name: Balance scale
desc: Equal-arm beam balances in Egypt and Mesopotamia allowed goods and metals to be weighed against standard masses.

name: Ruler
desc: Graduated measuring rods such as the copper-alloy Nippur cubit fixed lengths for building and trade.

name: Standard weights and measures
desc: State-sanctioned standard weights and lengths in Mesopotamia, Egypt and the Indus Valley made trade and taxation consistent.

name: Analytical balance
desc: Precision enclosed balances enabled the quantitative chemistry of Black and Lavoisier.

name: Calipers
desc: Sliding bronze calipers found in a Roman-era wreck measured thicknesses and diameters.

name: Vernier scale
desc: Pierre Vernier's auxiliary sliding scale let readings be taken to a fraction of the smallest main division.

name: Micrometer
desc: William Gascoigne's screw micrometer measured small angles in a telescope and later small lengths in workshops.

name: Metric system
desc: Revolutionary France defined decimal units of length and mass from natural references, later adopted worldwide.

name: International System of Units
desc: The 1960 General Conference on Weights and Measures established the modern SI as the global system of units.

name: Gnomon
desc: A vertical stick or pillar whose shadow tracked the sun's motion, the basis of sundials and early astronomy.

name: Sundial
desc: Egyptian shadow clocks divided daylight into hours using a gnomon's shadow on a marked surface.

name: Water clock
desc: Vessels that measured time by a regulated flow of water, used in Egypt, Babylon and China.

name: Hourglass
desc: A sand-filled glass timer, widely used at sea from the 14th century to time watches and speed logs.

name: Verge escapement
desc: The first mechanical escapement, releasing a gear train in regular steps, which made weight-driven clocks possible.

name: Mainspring
desc: A coiled steel spring that replaced weights as a clock's power source, allowing portable timepieces.

name: Pocket watch
desc: Spring-driven portable watches appeared in early 16th-century Germany and became common after the balance spring.

name: Pendulum
desc: Galileo's study of the pendulum's nearly constant period gave timekeeping its first precise natural regulator.

name: Pendulum clock
desc: Christiaan Huygens' pendulum clock cut timekeeping error from minutes to seconds per day.

name: Anchor escapement
desc: An escapement allowing small pendulum swings, which led to the accurate longcase clock.

name: Balance spring
desc: A fine spiral spring regulating a watch's balance wheel, which made pocket watches accurate to minutes a day.

name: Lever escapement
desc: Thomas Mudge's detached lever escapement became the standard mechanism in mechanical watches.

name: Marine chronometer
desc: John Harrison's H4 kept time at sea well enough to determine longitude, transforming navigation.

name: Wristwatch
desc: Watches worn on the wrist, first made by Patek Philippe and popularized by soldiers in the First World War.

name: Electric clock
desc: Alexander Bain's clock used electromagnets to drive a pendulum, enabling synchronized networks of clocks.

name: Piezoelectricity
desc: Pierre and Jacques Curie found that some crystals produce voltage under stress, the basis of quartz oscillators and sonar.

name: Quartz clock
desc: Warren Marrison and J. W. Horton's clock used a vibrating quartz crystal as a far steadier frequency reference.

name: Atomic clock
desc: The US National Bureau of Standards built the first clock referenced to an atomic transition, using ammonia.

name: Caesium atomic clock
desc: Louis Essen's caesium-beam clock at the National Physical Laboratory led to the 1967 atomic definition of the second.

name: Maser
desc: Charles Townes' ammonia maser amplified microwaves by stimulated emission, the forerunner of the laser.

name: Hydrogen maser
desc: A maser using hydrogen atoms that gives extremely stable short-term frequency for observatories and timekeeping.

name: Laser cooling
desc: Techniques using laser light to slow and cool atoms to microkelvin temperatures for precision measurement.

name: Optical frequency comb
desc: Mode-locked lasers producing evenly spaced frequencies let optical frequencies be counted directly against atomic clocks.

name: Optical lattice clock
desc: Clocks using atoms held in laser lattices reached accuracies of about one second in billions of years.

name: Magnifying glass
desc: Convex lenses used as reading aids were described by Roger Bacon in the 13th century.

name: Eyeglasses
desc: Spectacles for presbyopia appeared in Italy around 1286, extending the working lives of scholars and artisans.

name: Refracting telescope
desc: Kepler's convex-eyepiece design gave a wider field and became the basis of astronomical refractors.

name: Reflecting telescope
desc: Isaac Newton's telescope used a curved mirror to avoid the colour fringing of lenses.

name: Achromatic lens
desc: Combining crown and flint glass elements cancelled chromatic aberration, greatly improving telescopes and microscopes.

name: Spirit level
desc: Melchisédech Thévenot's sealed bubble vial gave a simple, precise indication of horizontal.

name: Segmented mirror telescope
desc: The Keck telescope combined computer-aligned hexagonal segments into a 10-metre mirror.

name: Adaptive optics
desc: Deformable mirrors correcting atmospheric turbulence in real time were first used on astronomical telescopes in 1989.

name: Astrophotography
desc: John William Draper's daguerreotype of the Moon began the photographic recording of the sky.

name: Fluorescence microscope
desc: Microscopes imaging light emitted by fluorescent samples, later central to cell biology.

name: Phase-contrast microscopy
desc: Frits Zernike's method turned phase shifts into contrast, letting living unstained cells be seen.

name: Confocal microscopy
desc: Marvin Minsky's pinhole design rejected out-of-focus light, enabling optical sectioning of thick samples.

name: Two-photon microscopy
desc: Pulsed-laser excitation allowed deep imaging of living tissue with less damage.

name: Super-resolution microscopy
desc: Methods such as STED and PALM broke the optical diffraction limit, earning the 2014 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

name: Electron microscope
desc: Ernst Ruska and Max Knoll built the first electron microscope using magnetic lenses to focus electrons.

name: Transmission electron microscopy
desc: Ruska's TEM exceeded the resolution of light microscopes by passing electrons through thin specimens.

name: Scanning electron microscope
desc: Manfred von Ardenne's scanning design imaged surfaces with a focused beam, commercialized in 1965.

name: Cryo-electron microscopy
desc: Imaging flash-frozen samples in vitreous ice allowed biomolecules to be resolved near atomic detail.

name: Scanning tunneling microscope
desc: Binnig and Rohrer's STM imaged individual atoms on surfaces using quantum tunnelling current.

name: Atomic force microscope
desc: A sharp probe on a cantilever mapped surface forces at nanometre scale, including on non-conducting samples.

name: Thermoscope
desc: Galileo's air thermoscope showed changes in temperature but had no fixed scale.

name: Thermometer
desc: Ferdinand II of Tuscany's sealed liquid-in-glass thermometer was independent of air pressure.

name: Mercury thermometer
desc: Daniel Fahrenheit's mercury thermometer with a reproducible scale made temperature readings comparable.

name: Pyrometer
desc: Josiah Wedgwood's clay-shrinkage pyrometer measured kiln temperatures beyond a thermometer's range.

name: Thermocouple
desc: Thomas Seebeck found that junctions of dissimilar metals produce voltage with temperature, now the most common temperature sensor.

name: Resistance thermometer
desc: William Siemens' platinum resistance thermometer measured temperature from electrical resistance.

name: Bolometer
desc: Samuel Langley's bolometer detected radiant heat, opening the infrared spectrum to measurement.

name: Barometer
desc: Evangelista Torricelli's mercury column measured air pressure and demonstrated a vacuum.

name: Hygrometer
desc: Nicholas of Cusa described weighing wool to gauge humidity, and later hair and dew-point hygrometers followed.

name: Anemometer
desc: Leon Battista Alberti described a swinging-plate wind gauge, later replaced by Robinson's cup anemometer.

name: Rain gauge
desc: Standardized bronze rain gauges were distributed across Joseon Korea to record rainfall.

name: Pitot tube
desc: Henri Pitot's tube measured flow speed from pressure, later used for aircraft airspeed.

name: Radiosonde
desc: Balloon-borne instruments radioing pressure, temperature and humidity, the backbone of upper-air forecasting.

name: Weather radar
desc: Radar adapted to detect precipitation, giving real-time tracking of storms.

name: Seismometer
desc: Zhang Heng's bronze seismoscope indicated the direction of distant earthquakes; modern seismographs followed in the 1880s.

name: Odometer
desc: Geared wheel counters described by Vitruvius and Heron measured distances travelled.

name: Surveying
desc: Egyptian rope stretchers measured land and laid out monuments, the origin of systematic surveying.

name: Groma
desc: A Roman cross-staff with plumb lines used to lay out straight roads and right-angle grids.

name: Dioptra
desc: A Greek sighting instrument for measuring angles in surveying and astronomy.

name: Triangulation
desc: Gemma Frisius described mapping by networks of measured angles, later used for national surveys.

name: Theodolite
desc: An instrument for measuring horizontal and vertical angles, central to geodetic surveying.

name: Armillary sphere
desc: Nested rings representing celestial circles, used to measure and demonstrate celestial positions.

name: Astrolabe
desc: A hand-held model of the sky used to find time, latitude and star positions, refined in the Islamic world.

name: Antikythera mechanism
desc: A Greek geared device that computed astronomical positions and eclipse cycles.

name: Quadrant
desc: A quarter-circle scale for measuring altitude angles, used in astronomy and navigation.

name: Jacob's staff
desc: Levi ben Gershon described this sliding-vane staff for measuring angles between celestial bodies.

name: Mariner's astrolabe
desc: A simplified heavy astrolabe used by Portuguese navigators to measure latitude at sea.

name: Backstaff
desc: John Davis' backstaff measured the sun's altitude by its shadow, sparing the navigator's eyes.

name: Chip log
desc: A knotted line timed with a sandglass to measure ship speed, the origin of the knot.

name: Dead reckoning
desc: Estimating position from known heading, speed and elapsed time, the basis of pre-modern navigation.

name: Octant
desc: John Hadley's double-reflecting octant measured angles accurately from a moving deck.

name: Sextant
desc: An extended reflecting instrument that measured lunar distances and altitudes for celestial navigation.

name: Gyroscope
desc: Léon Foucault named and used the gyroscope to demonstrate Earth's rotation.

name: Foucault pendulum
desc: A long free pendulum whose swing plane rotates, the first direct demonstration of Earth's rotation.

name: Gyrocompass
desc: Hermann Anschütz-Kaempfe's motor-driven gyroscope pointed to true north, unaffected by a steel hull's magnetism.

name: Accelerometer
desc: Instruments measuring proper acceleration, essential to inertial guidance and later in phones.

name: Inertial navigation system
desc: Gyroscopes and accelerometers computing position without outside references, first used on the V-2 rocket.

name: Ring laser gyroscope
desc: A gyroscope sensing rotation from the Sagnac effect in a laser loop, with no moving parts.

name: Radio direction finder
desc: Antennas finding the bearing of a radio transmitter, used for ship and aircraft navigation.

name: LORAN
desc: A hyperbolic radio navigation system timing pulses from shore stations to fix positions at sea.

name: Echo sounding
desc: Alexander Behm's method measured water depth by timing sound echoes from the seabed.

name: Sonar
desc: Active underwater sound ranging, developed in the First World War with piezoelectric quartz transducers.

name: Laser rangefinder
desc: Timing laser pulses to measure distance, first demonstrated by Hughes Aircraft in 1961.

name: Lidar
desc: Laser-based ranging and mapping, first used for atmospheric and lunar measurements.

name: Total station
desc: An electronic theodolite with built-in distance measurement and computation, now standard in surveying.

name: Electroscope
desc: William Gilbert's versorium detected static charge; Bennet's gold-leaf electroscope followed in 1787.

name: Galvanometer
desc: Johann Schweigger's coil-and-needle instrument detected and measured electric current.

name: Ammeter
desc: Moving-iron and moving-coil meters made current measurement practical for electrical engineering.

name: Multimeter
desc: Donald Macadie's AVO meter combined current, voltage and resistance measurement in one instrument.

name: Oscilloscope
desc: Ferdinand Braun's cathode-ray oscillograph displayed electrical waveforms over time.

name: Magnetometer
desc: Carl Friedrich Gauss built the first instrument for absolute measurement of magnetic field strength.

name: pH meter
desc: Arnold Beckman's electronic pH meter measured acidity precisely for chemistry and industry.

name: Dispersive prism
desc: Isaac Newton used glass prisms to show white light is a mixture of colours.

name: Diffraction grating
desc: Joseph von Fraunhofer's ruled wire and glass gratings measured wavelengths of light.

name: Fraunhofer lines
desc: Fraunhofer mapped dark lines in the solar spectrum, later explained as chemical signatures.

name: Spectroscope
desc: Kirchhoff and Bunsen's spectroscope identified elements by their spectral lines, discovering caesium and rubidium.

name: Astronomical spectroscopy
desc: William Huggins and Angelo Secchi used spectra to determine the composition of stars.

name: Infrared spectroscopy
desc: William Coblentz's infrared spectra of compounds made molecular structure identification possible.

name: Raman spectroscopy
desc: C. V. Raman's discovery of inelastic light scattering gave a new probe of molecular vibrations.

name: Spectrophotometer
desc: The Beckman DU made fast quantitative measurement of light absorption routine in laboratories.

name: Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy
desc: Interferometer-based infrared spectrometers using computed Fourier transforms greatly improved speed and sensitivity.

name: Mass spectrometry
desc: J. J. Thomson's parabola apparatus separated ions by mass, revealing isotopes of neon.

name: MALDI
desc: Laser desorption from a matrix ionized proteins and polymers for mass analysis.

name: Chromatography
desc: Mikhail Tsvet separated plant pigments on a column, founding chromatography.

name: Gas chromatography
desc: James and Martin's gas-liquid chromatography separated volatile compounds quickly and precisely.

name: Gas chromatography–mass spectrometry
desc: Coupling a gas chromatograph to a mass spectrometer allowed identification of substances in complex mixtures.

name: NMR spectroscopy
desc: Bloch and Purcell detected nuclear magnetic resonance in bulk matter, later the chemist's main structural tool.

name: Neutron diffraction
desc: Clifford Shull and Ernest Wollan used reactor neutrons to determine atomic and magnetic structures.

name: Michelson interferometer
desc: Albert Michelson's interferometer measured lengths to fractions of a wavelength and tested the ether hypothesis.

name: Fabry–Pérot interferometer
desc: A pair of parallel mirrors producing sharp interference fringes, later the resonator of lasers.

name: Holography
desc: Dennis Gabor invented holography to improve electron microscopy; lasers made it practical in 1962.

name: Optical tweezers
desc: Arthur Ashkin's focused laser beam trapped and moved particles and living cells.

name: Photomultiplier tube
desc: A vacuum tube multiplying photoelectrons to detect single photons.

name: Radio telescope
desc: Grote Reber's dish followed Karl Jansky's 1932 detection of cosmic radio waves and founded radio astronomy.

name: Aperture synthesis
desc: Martin Ryle combined signals from separated antennas to synthesize the resolution of a much larger telescope.

name: Very-long-baseline interferometry
desc: Telescopes thousands of kilometres apart recorded signals with atomic clocks and combined them later.

name: Event Horizon Telescope
desc: A planet-wide VLBI array that produced the first image of a black hole's shadow, in galaxy M87.

name: LIGO
desc: Kilometre-scale laser interferometers that made the first direct detection of gravitational waves in 2015.

name: Liquefaction of gases
desc: Cailletet and Pictet first liquefied oxygen, opening the field of cryogenics.

name: Hampson–Linde cycle
desc: A regenerative throttling process that made liquid air production practical and industrial.

name: Dewar flask
desc: James Dewar's double-walled vacuum vessel stored liquefied gases with little heat leak.

name: Liquefaction of helium
desc: Heike Kamerlingh Onnes liquefied helium at 4 K, enabling low-temperature physics.

name: Superconductivity
desc: Kamerlingh Onnes found that mercury loses all electrical resistance near absolute zero.

name: Dilution refrigerator
desc: A helium-3/helium-4 refrigerator reaching millikelvin temperatures continuously.

name: SQUID
desc: A superconducting loop with Josephson junctions, the most sensitive magnetometer known.

name: Superconducting magnet
desc: Niobium alloy wire carrying lossless current produced strong steady fields for accelerators and MRI.

name: Cloud chamber
desc: C. T. R. Wilson's chamber made tracks of charged particles visible as condensation trails.

name: Geiger counter
desc: The Geiger–Müller tube gave a simple, portable detector of ionizing radiation.

name: Scintillation counter
desc: Samuel Curran coupled a scintillating crystal to a photomultiplier to count radiation precisely.

name: Bubble chamber
desc: Donald Glaser's superheated-liquid detector recorded high-energy particle tracks in fine detail.

name: Wire chamber
desc: Georges Charpak's multiwire proportional chamber read particle tracks electronically at high rates.

name: Neutrino detector
desc: Cowan and Reines first detected neutrinos from a reactor using large liquid scintillator tanks.

name: Super-Kamiokande
desc: A giant water Cherenkov detector in Japan that discovered neutrino oscillations in 1998.

name: Cockcroft–Walton generator
desc: A voltage multiplier that accelerated protons to split lithium nuclei, the first artificial nuclear disintegration.

name: Linear particle accelerator
desc: Rolf Widerøe's linac accelerated ions with alternating fields along a straight line of drift tubes.

name: Cyclotron
desc: Ernest Lawrence's cyclotron accelerated particles in a spiral within a magnetic field.

name: Synchrotron
desc: An accelerator synchronizing its magnetic field with particle energy, allowing far higher energies.

name: Synchrotron light source
desc: Storage rings dedicated to producing intense X-rays for structural biology and materials science.

name: Particle collider
desc: Storage rings colliding opposing beams, beginning with AdA in Frascati, raised available collision energy.

name: Tevatron
desc: Fermilab's superconducting proton-antiproton collider discovered the top quark in 1995.

name: Large Hadron Collider
desc: CERN's 27-kilometre collider, the most powerful accelerator built, discovered the Higgs boson in 2012.

name: Steelyard balance
desc: An unequal-arm balance with a sliding counterweight that weighed heavy loads with a single small mass.

name: Spring scale
desc: A scale that measures weight by the extension of a steel spring, first made in Britain around 1770.

name: Gauge block
desc: Carl Edvard Johansson's precision steel blocks became the reference standard for workshop length measurement.

name: Kibble balance
desc: Bryan Kibble's watt balance related mass to electrical quantities and Planck's constant, enabling a new kilogram definition.

name: 2019 SI redefinition
desc: All SI base units were redefined by fixed values of physical constants, retiring the physical kilogram artefact.

name: Fusee
desc: A cone-shaped pulley that evened out a mainspring's declining force to keep spring clocks accurate.

name: Chronograph
desc: A watch with an independent stopwatch function, first built by Louis Moinet for astronomical timing.

name: Gridiron pendulum
desc: John Harrison's pendulum of alternating brass and steel rods compensated for thermal expansion.

name: Shortt–Synchronome clock
desc: A free-pendulum electromechanical clock that was the most accurate timekeeper until quartz clocks.

name: Chip-scale atomic clock
desc: NIST shrank an atomic frequency reference to a few cubic millimetres, enabling portable atomic timing.

name: Magneto-optical trap
desc: A device combining lasers and a magnetic field gradient to capture and cool clouds of neutral atoms.

name: Bose–Einstein condensate
desc: Cornell and Wieman first produced this ultracold state of matter in rubidium atoms in 1995.

name: Binoculars
desc: Ignazio Porro's prism erecting system made compact high-power binoculars possible.

name: Schmidt camera
desc: Bernhard Schmidt's wide-field telescope used a corrector plate to photograph large areas of sky sharply.

name: Coronagraph
desc: Bernard Lyot's instrument blocked the solar disc to observe the corona without an eclipse.

name: Transit instrument
desc: Ole Rømer's meridian telescope timed star crossings to fix celestial positions and correct clocks.

name: Spectroheliograph
desc: George Ellery Hale's instrument photographed the Sun in a single wavelength of light.

name: Orrery
desc: Geared models of the solar system demonstrated planetary motions for teaching.

name: Tide-predicting machine
desc: Lord Kelvin's machine summed harmonic components mechanically to forecast tides.

name: Planimeter
desc: A mechanical integrator that measures the area of a plane figure by tracing its boundary.

name: Oil immersion objective
desc: Immersing the objective in oil raised a microscope's numerical aperture and resolution.

name: Ultramicroscope
desc: Siedentopf and Zsigmondy's dark-field instrument revealed colloidal particles below the optical resolution limit.

name: Merkhet
desc: An Egyptian plumb-line sighting tool used to align buildings and time the night by star transits.

name: Torquetum
desc: A medieval astronomical instrument converting between celestial coordinate systems.

name: Weather vane
desc: Indicators of wind direction, notably the Triton on Athens' Tower of the Winds.

name: Hydrometer
desc: A floating instrument measuring liquid density, described in letters to Hypatia of Alexandria.

name: Thermographic camera
desc: Cameras imaging infrared radiation, first built by Kálmán Tihanyi and developed for military night use.

name: Decca Navigator System
desc: A British hyperbolic system using phase comparison of continuous radio signals, first used on D-Day.

name: Plane table
desc: A drawing board on a tripod used to plot survey maps directly in the field.

name: Gunter's chain
desc: Edmund Gunter's 66-foot measuring chain standardized land surveying in Britain and its colonies.

name: Tellurometer
desc: Trevor Wadley's microwave distance meter measured survey lines of tens of kilometres electronically.

name: Fibre-optic gyroscope
desc: A rotation sensor using light in a coil of optical fibre, compact and robust for navigation.

name: Wheatstone bridge
desc: A balanced circuit for precise resistance measurement, popularized by Charles Wheatstone.

name: Electron paramagnetic resonance
desc: Yevgeny Zavoisky detected resonant absorption by unpaired electrons in a magnetic field.

name: Electrospray ionization
desc: John Fenn's technique brought large biomolecules intact into a mass spectrometer.

name: High-performance liquid chromatography
desc: High-pressure columns made liquid chromatography fast and quantitative for pharmaceuticals and biochemistry.

name: Spark chamber
desc: A gas detector where sparks along particle paths recorded tracks, used to discover the muon neutrino.

name: Van de Graaff generator
desc: Robert Van de Graaff's belt-charged generator reached megavolt potentials for nuclear physics.

name: Betatron
desc: Donald Kerst's betatron accelerated electrons with a changing magnetic field.

name: Free-electron laser
desc: John Madey's laser generated tunable coherent light from relativistic electrons in an undulator.

name: Ultracentrifuge
desc: Theodor Svedberg's high-speed centrifuge measured the sizes of proteins and colloids.
